source_facts.summary: A seven-person group was reported to be climbing in the Yushan rear four peaks area on 2026-06-22.
Reports say the 57-year-old woman felt physically unwell or lacked strength and told teammates she would return to Yuanfeng Hut alone.
The rescue-summary text adds that the team paused near the Yushan South Peak trailhead four-way intersection while returning from Lushan toward Yuanfeng Hut.
Reports say teammates later did not find her at Yuanfeng Hut and requested rescue; the rescue-summary text says the guide searched and reported the incident.
The rescue-summary text reports dark and foggy conditions with poor visibility during the night search.
Reports say rescuers later found her deceased in a valley or steep-slope area near Yuanfeng Hut; official terrain details require human review.
The rescue-summary text says the body was packed and carried to Yuanfeng Hut, then hoisted by National Airborne Service Corps helicopter on 2026-06-24.

timeline.time_ref: 2026-06-22 return from Lushan toward Yuanfeng Hut

scout_implications.summary: Scout should treat a weak, tired, or symptomatic teammate requesting solo return as a team-separation risk that requires human review, companion assignment, contact confirmation, or whole-team retreat planning.

Scout pre-trip review should surface route workload, pace buffer, pack-load tolerance, offline map readiness, and satellite messenger availability as planning prompts, not as a medical or legal finding.
A field prompt could ask whether the returning member has an escort, confirmed route, communication method, last-known point, and explicit check-in deadline before separation is accepted.

If a member becomes missing, Scout should help humans package last-known point, intended destination, separation time, communication status, observed condition, weather, visibility, and search constraints for approved rescue communication.
Scout should keep darkness, fog, and visibility as review factors for late-day separation and retreat decisions, while leaving actual go/no-go authority to humans.

discussion_questions: Should Scout pre-trip and field prompts flag solo return by a tired or unwell teammate as a team-separation checkpoint requiring explicit human decision review?
What is the minimum evidence Scout should ask a team to record before any planned separation: escort, route, communication, last-known point, deadline, weather, and visibility?
How should Scout phrase help-seeking prompts so a tired team member can ask for assistance without framing it as failure or blame?
Should a dark/fog/poor-visibility condition automatically escalate a planned solo return to a whole-team retreat or escort-required review prompt?
